# Book I, Proposition 41

*The parallelogram is double of the triangle*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If a parallelogram have the same base with a triangle and be in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double of the triangle.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/41.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.41, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let the parallelogram ABCD have the same base BC with the triangle EBC, and let it be in the same parallels BC, AE;

I say that the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle BEC.

For let AC be joined.

Then the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle EBC; for it is on the same base BC with it and in the same parallels BC, AE. [I. 37]

But the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle ABC; for the diameter AC bisects it; [I. 34] so that the parallelogram ABCD is also double of the triangle EBC.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where the statement already gives a step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Already given.** "I say that the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle BEC." The statement gives the goal, and AC needs no drawing: `quadArea A B C D` already measures ABCD by its diameter AC, as the triangles ABC and ACD together.

```lean
/-- If a parallelogram have the same base with a triangle and be in the same parallels, the
parallelogram is double of the triangle. -/
theorem Prop41 {A B C D E : Point} (hABCD : Parallelogram A B C D) (hE : Collinear A D E) :
    quadArea A B C D = △ B E C + △ B E C := by
  -- For let the parallelogram ABCD have the same base BC with the triangle EBC,
  -- and let it be in the same parallels BC, AE;
  obtain ⟨AE, hA_AE, hD_AE, hE_AE⟩ := hE
  obtain ⟨BC, hB, hC⟩ := Postulate1 B C hABCD.2.1
  have hpar : Parallel AE BC := (hABCD.2.parallel hB hC hD_AE hA_AE).symm
  -- I say that the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle BEC.
  -- For let AC be joined.
  /- The area `quadArea A B C D` already measures ABCD by its diameter AC,
     as the triangles ABC and ACD together. -/
  -- Then the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle EBC;
  -- for it is on the same base BC with it and in the same parallels BC, AE. [I. 37]
  have hEBC : Triangle E B C :=
    (Triangle.of_line hB hC hABCD.2.1 (hpar.not_onLine hE_AE)).cab
  have h37 : △ A B C = △ E B C :=
    Prop37 hABCD.triangle hEBC ⟨AE, BC, hpar, hA_AE, hE_AE, hB, hC⟩
  -- But the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle ABC;
  -- for the diameter AC bisects it; [I. 34]
  have h34 : quadArea A B C D = △ A B C + △ A B C := Prop34.bisect hABCD
  -- so that the parallelogram ABCD is also double of the triangle EBC.
  rw [h34, h37, area_bac E B C]
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)

- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_of_on_inside_outside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L195): Two circles cut one another if the first passes through a point A inside the second, and a point B outside the second is inside or on the first. (Intersection 4, in LeanEuclid's corrected form)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)

- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`exists_point_on_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L29): Let a point be taken on the straight line L. (Points 2)

- [`inside_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L161): A circle is "convex": between two points on or inside it, every point is inside. (Circle 2)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (used here): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)

- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**Slide the vertex, halve the parallelogram.** Euclid joins AC and needs just two steps. I.37 slides the triangle's vertex from E to A along the parallel, and the diameter AC halves the parallelogram, by I.34. He uses the result at once: I.42 builds a parallelogram equal to a triangle with it, and in I.47 it makes each square on the sides, and each piece of the square on the base, double of a triangle.

**"By way of practice."** On this proposition Proclus considers "the area of a *trapezium* (a quadrilateral with only one pair of opposite sides parallel)", Heath reports (vol. 1, p. 338). He finds it less than double the triangle on its greater parallel side and more than double that on its lesser. Then he proves this: "*If a triangle be formed by joining the middle point of either of the non-parallel sides to the extremities of the opposite side, the area of the trapezium is always double of that of the triangle*" (vol. 1, p. 338).

**Why the middle point?** Proclus produces the straight line from one end of the opposite side through the middle point until it meets the other parallel side, produced. The two small triangles at the middle point are equal (I.26), so the trapezium is equal to one large triangle, and the triangle of the theorem is half of it, by I.38 (Heath, vol. 1, p. 339). Heath gathers Proclus' three results into one: the trapezium is greater than, equal to or less than double the triangle, as the middle point is on the greater parallel side, a side that is not parallel, or the lesser. The end of Proclus' note is lost, as Heath remarks under I.43.

**Where may E lie?** Our figure is Euclid's, with E on AD produced beyond D, but our statement lets E fall anywhere on the straight line AD, at A or at D among them. One argument serves for all, since our I.37 was stated with these cases in mind, and joining AC costs nothing: our area of a four-sided figure is already measured by a diameter.

**The modern way.** Let b = C − B; then D − A = b, and E = A + t·b for some real number t. With the cross product of I.35, the parallelogram has area |b × (A − B)|, while EBC has area ½|b × (E − B)| = ½|b × (A − B)|, since b × b = 0.

## Further reading

- For the cross products of the modern way grown into one formula for any polygon, Bart Braden's ["The Surveyor's Area Formula"](https://web.archive.org/web/20140629065751/https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/pubs/Calc_Articles/ma063.pdf) (1986, free online), a friendly article on the "shoelace" formula: give it the corners of a field and it hands back the area.
- For more cutting and rebuilding like Proclus' trapezium, which becomes a triangle when one triangle is moved, Greg N. Frederickson's [*Dissections: Plane & Fancy*](https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/gnf/book.html) (1997), a gorgeous picture book of figures cut into pieces that rebuild other figures.
